title: Meter parts out of a feed chute with a two-stop escapement, keeping the red part back
instruction: Use the two stops on the feed chute to release, one at a time, every part ahead of the red one into the bin, then leave the red part in the chute with both hands off the stops.
context: Gravity feed chutes on assembly and machining lines hand out one part at a time with a two-stop escapement: one stop holds the queue while the other lets the first part go. Open both together and the whole queue runs out.
setup: Positions in cm from the midpoint between the two arm bases (61 cm apart), x forward, y left; heights from the table top (74.75 cm above the floor). Chute: fixed dark grey steel, sloping 8 degrees down toward -y, centred at x = 24, inside 5.4 wide, 43 long; its floor's low end at y = -6, height 6, its high end at y = 36.6, height 12, closed; walls 0.5 thick; two steel legs. A cover over it from 7 cm along the chute (measured from the low end) to the high end leaves a 3 cm slot along its centre, its underside 2.8 above the floor. Parts: six aluminium blocks, 5 x 5 cm and 2.5 tall, 150 g, each with a 2 x 0.8 x 1 cm nose low on its downhill face, nose against the block ahead, so neighbouring blocks stand 8 mm apart; five are silver and one is red; the first rests against the lower stop with its centre at y = 4.9, height 7.5. Lower stop: orange, a 1.6 wide, 6 mm thick plate through the slot, at 8.5 cm along the chute, sprung shut with its tip 1.2 above the floor; a see-saw lever on a pivot beside the chute joins it to a 5 x 5 cm pad, 1 thick, at x = 30.5, y = -8, top 9.8 high; pressing the pad down about 1.9 cm, to its stop, lifts the plate's tip clear of the blocks. Upper stop: blue, a 1.6 wide, 5 mm thick pin at 13.9 cm along the chute, in the gap between the first and second blocks, sprung up with its tip 3 above the floor; a 5 x 5 cm pad, 1 thick, at x = 30.5, y = 6.8, top 14.9 high; pressing the pad down 1.8 cm, to its stop, drops the tip to 1.2 above the floor. Bin: fixed blue plastic, centred at (24, -13.5), 12 x 14 cm inside, 1 cm walls rising 4 above the table, 0.4 cm floor, under the chute's low end. Lots (one per trial): the red part is 2nd in the queue in A, 3rd in B, 4th in C, 5th in D, counting from the lower stop. The screenshot shows A.
scoring: Terms. In the bin: centre inside its walls and at most 5 cm above their tops, still (under 1 cm/s), stacked or tipped included. Red held: the red block's centre inside the chute's walls and at least 2.3 cm uphill of the lower stop's face. Hands clear: each gripper's fingertip midpoint 6 cm or more from the top centre of both pads. Read at the end of the run (no early end). Score: 0 if the red part isn't held. 1.0 if the parts in the bin are exactly the parts ahead of the red one, every part has been still (under 1 cm/s and 0.5 rad/s) for the last 1 s, and both hands are clear. 0.15 if the red part is held, at least one part is in the bin, and the count is one short of the parts ahead, or is exact with a hand not clear or a part not yet still for 1 s. Otherwise 0. A part anywhere else counts for nothing. The parts keep their order in the chute, so a part in the bin is always one from ahead of the red one. The task's score is the mean over one trial of each lot; a fixed count that never reads the queue averages at most 0.29, and with no early end it can't stop itself at the right count. On real arms: count the bin's parts and check the red part from a top-down photo after the arms withdraw.
reset_notes: Close both stops as sprung, slide the parts back up through the chute's low end in the next lot's order (A, B, C, D in turn), and let them rest nose to tail against the lower stop.
fidelity: Approximate. Parts slide on low friction (0.05) in place of rollers or a polished track; the stops are rigid plates and pins on spring-return joints with no spring parts modelled; the springs and pad forces are typical of light hand-worked stops, not measured from one machine. Blocks' noses keep a gap for the upper pin; real chutes often use part shape or a wedge for the same job. Four fixed lots, chosen at the start.
